     The Light at Cape Verrick                                                                                          
                                                                                                                        
     Maren had kept the light at Cape Verrick for nineteen years, and in all that time she had learned that the sea     
     did not care about the things people believed about it.                                                            
                                                                                                                        
     On the morning the fog came — the kind that swallowed the whole headland and made the world no larger than the     
     room you stood in — she climbed the one hundred and twelve steps with the thermos in her left hand and the         
     logbook under her arm, and she did not hurry, because hurrying had killed more keepers than storms had.            
                                                                                                                        
     The lamp had been converted to automatic acetylene two years before, which meant the machine would do its job      
     whether she believed in it or not. She checked the pressure by hand anyway. Nine pounds, steady as a pulse. She    
     wound the clockwork that turned the lens, because that was still hers. The great lens began its slow revolution,   
     a bar of white light sweeping the fog like a hand feeling its way across a table.                                  
                                                                                                                        
     At the top of the stairs the wind came in through the gallery rail and made a sound she had never learned to       
     name. It was not a moan. It was not a voice. But it went through her the way voices used to.                       
                                                                                                                        
     Below and seaward, the fishing fleet had gone out at four in the morning, and the town had already gone quiet      
     behind her

I'll write the story now.                                                                                          
                                                                                                                        
     The Light at Cape Verrick                                                                                          
                                                                                                                        
     Maren had kept the light at Cape Verrick for nineteen years, and in all that time she had learned that the sea     
     did not care about the things people believed about it.                                                            
                                                                                                                        
     On the morning the fog came — the kind that swallowed the whole headland and made the world no larger than the     
     room you stood in — she climbed the one hundred and twelve steps with the thermos in her left hand and the         
     logbook under her arm, and she did not hurry, because hurrying had killed more keepers than storms had.            
                                                                                                                        
     The lamp had been converted to automatic acetylene two years before, which meant the machine would do its job      
     whether she believed in it or not. She checked the pressure by hand anyway. Nine pounds, steady as a pulse. She    
     wound the clockwork that turned the lens, because that was still hers. The great lens began its slow revolution,   
     a bar of white light sweeping the fog like a hand feeling its way across a table.                                  
                                                                                                                        
     At the top of the stairs the wind came in through the gallery rail and made a sound she had never learned to       
     name. It was not a moan. It was not a voice. But it went through her the way voices used to.                       
                                                                                                                        
     Below and seaward, the fishing fleet had gone out at four in the morning, and the town had already gone quiet      
     behind her, and the only other living thing within a mile was a herring gull named Six, who had claimed the        
     gallery railing three winters ago and whom she fed, against all regulation, on the crusts she pretended not to     
     bring.                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                        
     She wrote in the logbook the way she always did. Wind: northeast, freshening. Sea: moderate, long swell from the   
     northwest. Visibility: nil. Lit the lamp at 06:14. Nothing burning, nothing wrong, the ordinary sentence of a      
     woman keeping a light for nobody in particular.                                                                    
                                                                                                                        
     By noon the fog had thinned to a grey gauze and the lens threw its light thirty feet and stopped. The cliff path   
     below had become a rumour. The gulls had gone somewhere inland.
